chapterBreakdown.gentle:
A strategy can be commercially sound and still stall inside the organization. The idea may make sense, but people may not see the urgency, resources may stay stuck in old uses, key contributors may not move, and internal blockers may slow the work. That means execution can fail even after the strategy itself has earned the right to continue. A good move can still sit still for too long, even while leaders think they already chose it and approved it fully internally.

Kim and Mauborgne answer that problem with tipping point leadership. The point is not to change everything at once. It is to focus on the few hurdles that keep the strategy from moving: cognitive, resource, motivational, and political hurdles. The chapter matters because it turns vague resistance into a smaller set of bottlenecks that leaders can actually confront.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
A strong strategy can still die in the institution meant to carry it. The move may pass the commercial test, yet people still do not grasp why it matters, resources remain locked in older priorities, the few people who need to move stay still, and internal blockers keep the effort from gaining traction. Execution failure is not always proof that the strategy was weak. It may be proof that the organization never moved. That difference should change the response before leadership wastes more energy, time, attention, momentum, and trust.

This chapter answers that problem with tipping point leadership. Its logic is concentrated leverage, not broad reform. Kim and Mauborgne narrow the execution challenge into four hurdles: cognitive, resource, motivational, and political. The chapter matters because it shows leaders where to aim effort instead of letting resistance remain a foggy excuse.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A blue-ocean move can survive the market and still get killed by its own organization. People keep acting as if nothing changed, resources stay chained to yesterday, the few actors who matter never move, and quiet internal blockers slow the strategy until momentum dies. That is not just bad luck. It is what happens when leaders talk about execution in generalities instead of attacking the real bottlenecks. Drift wins when no one names the choke point, the blocker, or the real source of drag.

Kim and Mauborgne answer with tipping point leadership. The point is not to inspire everyone equally or reform the whole institution at once. It is to hit the few hurdles that actually stop movement: cognitive, resource, motivational, and political hurdles. The chapter matters because it turns organizational drag into named targets instead of letting resistance hide behind vague leadership language.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
A strategy can clear the commercial gate and still fail to move the organization. The buyer value may be real, the economics may hold, and the adoption path may look plausible, yet execution still stalls. People may not grasp why the change matters, scarce resources may remain trapped in old routines, the people whose behavior matters most may stay untouched, and internal blockers may quietly slow the move. That is the pressure opening Chapter 7.

Kim and Mauborgne do not treat this as a vague problem of culture or attitude. They narrow it. The organization usually does not need to be transformed everywhere at once. It needs movement through a few decisive hurdles that keep the strategy from becoming real. Once those hurdles are named, leadership stops wasting energy on broad symbolic reform and starts looking for leverage.

The public frame is tipping point leadership. Its logic is concentrated effort where a smaller intervention can unlock wider movement. The chapter therefore rejects the fantasy that execution is solved by inspiration spread evenly across the institution. Instead, it asks where the bottleneck truly sits and what kind of barrier is creating it.

Those barriers stay distinct. Cognitive hurdles appear when people do not yet see why the strategic move matters. Resource hurdles appear when scarce means remain tied to familiar activities. Motivational hurdles appear when the people whose movement matters most have not been shifted strongly enough to act. Political hurdles appear when threatened interests or hidden blockers can still slow the strategy. The chapter matters because it keeps those hurdles separate instead of flattening them into one idea of resistance.

That distinction changes the leadership job. The task is not to do more everywhere. It is to attack the few leverage points strong enough to move the rest. Once the organization can move through those hurdles, the question changes again. Execution no longer depends only on clearing bottlenecks. It starts to depend on whether the strategy process itself can hold commitment across the wider organization.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The hidden risk after Chapter 6 is assuming that a commercially coherent move will now execute on its own. Chapter 7 exists because that assumption fails. A strategy can make sense in the market and still stall inside the organization. People may not understand the need for change, resources may remain attached to older priorities, the few actors whose behavior matters most may stay still, and internal blockers may make progress costly. The strategy may be sound while the institution remains inert.

Kim and Mauborgne answer that problem by narrowing execution into a few named hurdles. This is not broad change-management language. It is targeted diagnosis. The organization usually does not need universal reform before it can move. It needs leadership that identifies the bottleneck and applies effort where movement will spread. That is why the chapter's public mechanism is tipping point leadership rather than diffuse organizational renewal.

The four hurdles define the work. Cognitive hurdles mean people do not yet grasp the strategic reality. Resource hurdles mean scarce means still feed old activity instead of high-leverage action. Motivational hurdles mean the critical people have not been moved strongly enough to act. Political hurdles mean internal interests can still obstruct the strategy. The chapter matters because it prevents leaders from using the word resistance as a lazy summary for very different problems.

That distinction also changes what counts as good leadership. If the issue is cognitive, the move is to make reality harder to ignore. If the issue is resources, the move is to concentrate scarce means instead of pleading for more. If the issue is motivation, the move is to focus on the few people or units whose behavior shifts everyone else. If the issue is politics, the move is to identify blockers early instead of pretending execution is neutral.

The chapter's hard edge is that diffuse reform can feel serious while leaving the real bottleneck untouched. A strong strategy still dies if leaders spread effort too thinly, confuse morale with movement, or ignore the interests that can quietly strangle execution. Tipping point leadership matters because it accepts scarcity and opposition, then looks for leverage rather than excuses.

That is the bridge to the next chapter. Once the organization can move through its key hurdles, leadership still has to build execution into strategy itself. Chapter 7 clears the barriers that stop motion. Chapter 8 asks how commitment becomes durable enough to last.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A lot of strategies do not fail in the market first. They die in the institution that approved them. The move may already deserve to live commercially, but people keep treating it like a side project, resources stay chained to yesterday, the few actors who could shift the system never move, and quiet internal blockers keep draining momentum. Then leadership calls the whole mess resistance and acts as if naming the fog counted as progress.

Kim and Mauborgne attack that laziness by narrowing execution into a few decisive hurdles. Chapter 7 is not interested in general culture talk. It is interested in leverage. The organization does not have to be transformed everywhere at once. It has to move where the bottleneck is real. That is why the chapter's governing idea is tipping point leadership rather than broad reform theater.

The four hurdles are the map. Cognitive hurdles keep people blind to why the move matters. Resource hurdles keep scarce means feeding old routines. Motivational hurdles keep the few people who matter most from acting. Political hurdles let threatened interests or hidden blockers slow the strategy without having to argue against it openly. The chapter matters because it strips resistance of its vagueness and turns it into named targets.

That shift changes the leadership job immediately. If people do not see, make the reality unavoidable. If resources are trapped, concentrate what exists where it can shift the system. If motivation is weak, move the few whose behavior changes everyone else's sense of what is possible. If politics is the barrier, stop pretending execution is clean and surface the blockers before they bury the strategy.

The chapter's real warning is that diffuse reform feels noble because it spreads effort widely, but wide effort often protects the true bottleneck. Leaders can mistake motion for movement, budget talk for leverage, and morale language for actual execution. Chapter 7 matters because it makes that self-deception harder. It tells leaders to stop treating the whole institution as the unit of work when only a few points truly decide whether the move lives.

Then the chapter hands the problem forward. Once the organization can move, the next question is not simply how to push harder. The next question is how strategy and execution become tied tightly enough that follow-through holds after the bottlenecks break.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
A strategy can become commercially coherent before the organization is ready to move. The buyer value may be real, the economics may hold, and the opportunity may deserve commitment. Yet the institution still stalls. People may not understand why change is necessary, scarce resources may remain tied to older routines, the few people whose movement matters most may stay untouched, and internal blockers may quietly slow the move until momentum dies. A sound strategy can therefore fail inside the system meant to carry it.

Kim and Mauborgne answer that gap by narrowing execution into a few decisive hurdles. They do not treat resistance as a vague cultural cloud. They treat it as a set of bottlenecks that leadership can identify and attack. That shift matters because diffuse change language invites diffuse effort. Once the barriers are named, leadership no longer has to pretend that broad reform everywhere is the only serious response.

The chapter's public mechanism is tipping point leadership. Its force lies in concentrated leverage. A leader does not begin by trying to change every process, every person, and every assumption at once. The leader looks for where limited effort can unlock wider movement across the system. That makes execution strategic. The institution stops being a mysterious wall and becomes a map of a few leverage points and a few barriers that matter more than the rest.

Those barriers remain distinct for a reason. Cognitive hurdles mean people still do not see the strategic reality clearly enough to move. Resource hurdles mean scarce means remain committed to inherited priorities rather than high-leverage work. Motivational hurdles mean the people whose behavior matters most have not been moved strongly enough to act. Political hurdles mean threatened interests, hidden blockers, or internal opposition can still slow the strategy even when its logic is sound. The chapter becomes sharper the moment those hurdles stop being blended together.

That distinction changes what leadership must do. If the problem is cognitive, the task is to make the strategic facts harder to ignore. If the problem is resources, the task is to concentrate what exists instead of complaining first about what is missing. If the problem is motivation, the task is to move the few people or units whose action changes wider behavior. If the problem is political, the task is to identify and confront blockers early rather than pretend execution sits above power. The chapter matters because it replaces generalized effort with matched intervention.

Its hard edge is that diffuse reform often feels responsible while protecting the real bottleneck. Leaders can spread attention widely, praise commitment, and request more budget while the decisive hurdle stays untouched. They can call the atmosphere resistant while refusing to name whether the barrier is blindness, scarcity, weak motivation, or political obstruction. The chapter is disciplined because it treats that vagueness as part of the failure, not as a neutral description of it.

Once the organization can move through its key hurdles, the next question changes. The issue is no longer only how to break the bottleneck. The issue becomes how strategy and execution get tied together so commitment survives after the narrow leverage move has done its work. That is the handoff to the next chapter. Movement has begun, but durable follow-through still has to be built.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The hidden danger after strategic sequence is institutional inertia. A move can deserve to live commercially and still die inside the organization. People may not see why the strategy matters, scarce resources may remain trapped in old work, the few actors whose movement would shift the system may stay still, and internal blockers may make progress costly without openly opposing it. Chapter 7 exists because commercially coherent strategy does not execute itself.

That narrowing matters because diffuse explanations produce diffuse effort. Once the bottleneck is visible, leadership can stop performing seriousness everywhere and start applying leverage where movement actually spreads.

The chapter's governing mechanism is tipping point leadership. It is not broad organizational uplift. It is concentrated force at the points where limited intervention changes wider behavior. For that reason the chapter matters after Chapter 6. Commercial viability cleared the move to continue. Chapter 7 asks how the institution itself gets cleared to carry it.

The four hurdles define the job precisely. Cognitive hurdles keep people blind to strategic reality. Resource hurdles keep scarce means attached to inherited priorities. Motivational hurdles keep the critical people or units from acting. Political hurdles let threatened interests or hidden blockers slow the move without having to defeat it openly. The chapter matters because it prevents leaders from using one lazy word, resistance, to describe four very different problems.

That distinction also changes what counts as competent leadership. Cognitive barriers require exposure to reality, not more abstract explanation. Resource barriers require concentration, not automatic pleas for expansion. Motivational barriers require focusing on the few actors whose movement changes the rest. Political barriers require identifying opponents and blockers early, before quiet obstruction hardens into delay. The chapter's leverage comes from matching the intervention to the real barrier instead of repeating the same leadership ritual at every obstacle.

Its sharper warning is that diffuse reform can look ethical, balanced, and serious while still protecting the real bottleneck. Leaders can spread effort widely, celebrate morale, and talk about alignment while the decisive hurdle stays untouched. They can even call the strategy hard to execute without admitting whether the institution is blind, resource-starved in the wrong places, weakly motivated at the key nodes, or politically obstructed. Chapter 7 matters because it makes that evasiveness harder to sustain.

Once the bottlenecks begin to break, the execution problem changes again. The question is no longer only how to force motion through a few leverage points. The question becomes how to build commitment and follow-through into the strategy process itself. Chapter 8 follows because narrow leverage starts movement, but durable execution still requires a wider process that people can accept and carry. The institution has to keep moving after the choke point opens. Otherwise the early motion fades before the strategy can take root.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A lot of strategies do not die because the move was weak. They die because the institution never moved. The idea may already deserve to live commercially, yet people keep treating it like a side issue, resources stay chained to yesterday, the few actors who could shift the system never act, and quiet internal blockers keep draining momentum until leadership mistakes slow death for normal friction. That is the enemy in Chapter 7.

Kim and Mauborgne attack that enemy by stripping execution of its comforting vagueness. Resistance is not a mood. It is a handful of bottlenecks. Chapter 7 refuses to let leaders hide behind culture talk, alignment slogans, or broad reform plans that spread effort everywhere and clear nothing. Once the barrier is named, leverage has somewhere to land.

That is why tipping point leadership governs the chapter. Its logic is concentrated force, not universal uplift. The organization does not need heroic transformation in every corner before the strategy can move. It needs leaders who can identify where a small intervention changes wider behavior and where the true choke point is hiding. That is what makes the chapter dangerous to lazy leadership language.

The four hurdles are the map. Cognitive hurdles keep people blind. Resource hurdles keep scarce means feeding the wrong work. Motivational hurdles keep the few people who matter most from acting. Political hurdles let threatened interests or quiet blockers slow the move without having to argue against it publicly. That distinction changes the job immediately. If blindness is the barrier, make reality unavoidable. If resources are trapped, concentrate what exists where it can move the system. If motivation is weak, move the few whose behavior rewrites everyone else's expectations. If politics is the problem, stop pretending execution is clean and surface the blockers before they suffocate the move. Chapter 7 is ruthless because it asks leaders to stop spraying effort across the institution and start fighting at the point that decides the outcome.

Its hardest warning is that broad reform often protects the true bottleneck by surrounding it with noise. Leaders can spend money, schedule meetings, praise commitment, and widen participation while the decisive barrier remains untouched. They can call the atmosphere difficult because that sounds wiser than admitting that the institution is blind, misallocated, weakly moved at the key nodes, or politically compromised. Then the problem tightens again. Once the choke points crack, execution still does not become safe. The institution now has motion, but motion can decay unless the process itself earns commitment and clarity. That is the handoff to Chapter 8. Tipping point leadership starts the movement. plan.gentle: If a shared project keeps slowing down, then focus on the one barrier whose removal would unlock wider movement.
plan.direct: If personal follow-through is weak, then look for the few actors or blockers that matter most.
plan.competitive: If the project is stuck, hit the point that moves the rest.

front.direct: What can still fail after the commercial test passes?
front.competitive: What kills the move after the market says yes?

back.gentle: The organization can still stall even when the strategy is sound.

back.competitive: The institution can still choke the move.

front.gentle: What is tipping point leadership doing here?

back.gentle: It focuses effort where small leverage can unlock wider movement.
back.direct: Tipping point leadership means concentrated leverage against decisive hurdles.
back.competitive: It hits the choke point instead of reforming everything.

front.direct: Which execution barriers does the chapter name?
front.competitive: What are the four faces of drag?

back.gentle: The chapter names four execution barriers: seeing the need, freeing the means, moving the key people, and handling blockers.

back.competitive: Blindness, trapped means, unmoved key actors, and blockers with interests.

front.gentle: Why does the chapter keep the hurdles distinct?

back.competitive: Once everything is resistance, nothing gets hit precisely.

back.gentle: The next issue is building execution into strategy so commitment lasts.
back.direct: After leverage starts motion, the process itself has to support durable follow-through.
back.competitive: Breaking the blockers starts movement; the next fight is keeping commitment alive.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: A sound strategy still stalls if the organization cannot move through its cognitive, resource, motivational, and political hurdles.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: Chapter 7 argues that leaders must identify the real bottleneck and apply concentrated leverage instead of spreading reform everywhere.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: If the move deserves to live, stop feeding the atmosphere and hit the choke point that decides whether it moves.
